== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|12=draft}} <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines-->
<!--広川町)-->

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

revision.text:
本項目では、[[和歌山県]][[有田郡]][[広川町 (和歌山県)|広川町]]に所在する'''九十九王子'''（くじゅうくおうじ）について述べる。
== 九十九王子とは == {{Main|九十九王子}}
九十九王子（くじゅうくおうじ）とは、[[熊野古道]]、特に[[紀伊路|紀伊路・中辺路]]沿いに在する[[神社]]のうち、主に[[12世紀]]から [[13世紀]]にかけて、皇族・貴人の熊野詣に際して先達をつとめた熊野修験の手で急速に組織された一群の神社をいい、参詣者の守護が祈願された。
しかしながら、[[1221年]]（[[承久]]3年）の[[承久の乱]]以降、[[京都|京]]からの熊野詣が下火になり、そのルートであった紀伊路が衰退するとともに、荒廃と退転がすすんだ。[[室町時代]]以降、熊野詣がかつてのような卓越した地位を失うにつれ、この傾向はいっそう進み、[[江戸時代|近世]][[紀州藩]]の手による顕彰も行なわれたものの、勢いをとどめるまでには至らなかった。さらに、[[明治]]以降の[[神道]]の[[国家神道]]化とそれに伴う合祀、市街化による廃絶などにより、旧社地が失われたり、比定地が不明になったものも多い。
本記事では、これら九十九王子のうち、比定地が広川町にある王子を扱う。
== 広川町の九十九王子 == 広川町の九十九王子は3社。
=== 井関王子 === {{multiple image |align = right |width1 = 150 |image1 = 津兼王子跡.jpeg |caption1 = 井関（津兼）王子跡 |- |width2 = 150 |image2 = 丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg |caption2 = 丹賀大権現に合祀されている井関王子 |- }} [[九十九王子の (海南市)#久米崎王子|久米崎王子]]から広川に沿って南下し、広川東岸の[[湯浅御坊道路]]料金所のかたわらに'''井関王子'''（いせきおうじ）の跡地がある。「熊野道之間愚記」（『[[明月記]]』所収）[[建仁]]元年（[[1201年]]）10月10日条に「次参井関王子、於此所雨漸休」とあり、参詣の後、雨を避けて休息をとったとある<ref name="Kadokawa_1985_118">「角川日本地名大辞典」編纂委員会[1985: 118]</ref>。
[[江戸時代]]後期[[紀州藩]]が編纂した地誌『[[紀伊続風土記]]』には、社地は村の北の入口にあり、周囲82[[間]]であったと伝え、続けて、社地の字にちなんで「'''津兼王子'''」と呼ばれていると述べており<ref name="heibon_1997_90">平凡社[1997: 90]</ref>、他に『紀伊名所図会』にも同様の記述が見られる<ref name="Kadokawa_1985_118"/>。これは当地に井関王子以外にも津兼王子があったとする伝承があり、この2社の異同に関する異説があったことによるものである。『紀伊続風土記』や『紀伊名所図会』は両社が同一説を採るが、2社が別々の社であったとする説もある。後者の説によれば、井関王子址の東300メートルの地が津兼王子址であり、街道筋が西よりに付け替えられたことにより、井関王子が成立したのだという<ref name="heibon_1997_90"/>。
[[明治時代|明治期]]に井関の稲荷明神社祭礼の際の御旅所とされ、村有の耕作地を社地の一部に取り込んで拡張したが、[[1909年]]（[[明治]]42年）に稲荷明神社とともに上津木八幡神社に合祀された<ref name="heibon_1997_90"/>。[[西律]]が[[1971年]]（昭和46年）に調査した際には、陶製の小さな祠がミカン畑のなかにあった<ref>西[1987: 116]</ref>が、湯浅御坊道路の工事で社地は完全に失われた<ref>長谷川[2007: 83]</ref>。
近隣の丹賀大権現に合祀されている。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町3113-1
=== 河瀬王子 === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|河瀬王子]] 井関王子から南下し、河瀬橋を渡った広川西岸にあるのが'''河瀬王子'''（ごのせおうじ）の跡地である。
「熊野道之間愚記」建仁元年（1201年）10月10日条に、井関王子についで「ツノセ王子」に参拝したとあり、『[[民経記]]』承元4年（1210年）4 月26日条には「角瀬川」と見える。しかし、この王子の呼称には異説が多く、西によれば川瀬王子（かわせおうじ、『紀伊続風土記』『紀伊名所図会』）、津の瀬王子（つのせおうじ、[[応永]]34年〈[[1427年]]〉の『熊野詣日記』）、角瀬王子（『南紀神社録』）などがあり、『和歌山県聖蹟』は「熊野道之間愚記」を根拠にツノセを本来の名としている<ref>西[1987: 117]</ref>。[[1908年]]（明治41年）に上津木八幡神社に合祀された<ref>長谷川[2007: 84]</ref>。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町河瀬143
=== 馬留王子 === 河瀬王子から南下し、鹿瀬（ししがせ）山麓にあるのが'''馬留王子'''（うまどめおうじ）の跡地である。「熊野道之間愚記」、『[[中右記]]』、さらに応永34年（1427年）の『熊野詣日記』にも記述が見えないことから、これらの参詣記の年代以降に成立したと見られる。しかし、『紀伊続風土記』は馬留の名の由来を、熊野御幸の時代に、この先の鹿瀬峠が険しいために馬で越えることが出来ず、馬を留めたことにあるとしている<ref>平凡社 [1997: 115]</ref>。[[1942年]]（[[昭和]]17年）の『[[和歌山県聖蹟]]』には、1メートル角位の小さな社<ref>長谷川[2007: 85]</ref>や数個の階段石、社殿跡と見られる玉砂利があったというが、1971年（昭和46年）に西が調査した際には、一帯はミカン畑となっており何もなかったという<ref>西[1987: 118]</ref>。[[日高郡 (和歌山県)|日高郡]][[日高町 (和歌山県)|日高町]]にある同名の[[九十九王子 (日高町)#馬留王子|馬留王子]]と区別するために、広川町の馬留王子を東ノ馬留王子、日高町の馬留王子を西ノ馬留王子と称することがある<ref>長谷川[2007: 85-87]</ref>。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町399
== 周辺情報 == 馬留王子（東ノ馬留王子）から次の沓掛王子（日高町）の間にあるのが[[鹿ヶ瀬峠]]になる。紀伊路の中では珍しく石畳路が残されており、大峠と小峠の二つのピークを越えると日高町となる。以下の画像では峠を越えた日高町側も掲出する。 <gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|鹿ヶ瀬峠への道 File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|峠の頂上「法華の壇」 File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|鹿ヶ瀬峠からの道（日高町） File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|路傍の題目板碑（日高町） </gallery>
== 注 == {{Reflist|2}}
== 文献 == * 「[[角川日本地名大辞典]]」編纂委員会編、1985、『和歌山県』、角川書店（角川日本地名大辞典30） ISBN 404001300X * [[西律|西 律]]、1987、『熊野古道みちしるべ - 熊野九十九王子現状踏査録』、荒尾成文堂（みなもと選書1） * 長谷川 靖高、2007、『熊野王子巡拝ガイドブック』、新風書房 ISBN 9784882696292 * [[平凡社]]編、1997、『大和・紀伊寺院神社大事典』、平凡社 ISBN 458213402-5
== 関連項目 == {{Commonscat|Kujuku-ojis|九十九王子}} * [[熊野信仰]] * [[熊野古道]] - [[紀伊路]] * [[九十九王子]] ** （[[九十九王子 (湯浅町)#久米崎王子|久米崎王子]]） - '''井関王子''' - '''河瀬王子''' - '''馬留王子''' - （[[九十九王子 (日高町)#沓掛王子|沓掛王子]]）
== 外部リンク == * [http://www.town.hirogawa.wakayama.jp/kankou/kumanokodou.html 熊野古道] - 広川町役場公式サイト内。 {{-}} {{九十九王子}} {{神道 横}} {{DEFAULTSORT:くしゆうくおうしひろかわちよう}} [[Category:九十九王子|ひろかわ]] [[Category:和歌山県の神社]] [[Category:和歌山県広川町の建築物]] [[Category:和歌山県広川町の歴史]]

== 広川町の九十九王子 == 広川町の九十九王子は3社。
=== 井関王子 === {{multiple image |align = right |width1 = 150 |image1 = 津兼王子跡.jpeg |caption1 = 井関（津兼）王子跡 |- |width2 = 150 |image2 = 丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg |caption2 = 丹賀大権現に合祀されている井関王子 |- }} [[九十九王子の (海南市)#久米崎王子|久米崎王子]]から広川に沿って南下し、広川東岸の[[湯浅御坊道路]]料金所のかたわらに'''井関王子'''（いせきおうじ）の跡地がある。「熊野道之間愚記」（『[[明月記]]』所収）[[建仁]]元年（[[1201年]]）10月10日条に「次参井関王子、於此所雨漸休」とあり、参詣の後、雨を避けて休息をとったとある<ref name="Kadokawa_1985_118">「角川日本地名大辞典」編纂委員会[1985: 118]</ref>。
[[江戸時代]]後期[[紀州藩]]が編纂した地誌『[[紀伊続風土記]]』には、社地は村の北の入口にあり、周囲82[[間]]であったと伝え、続けて、社地の字にちなんで「'''津兼王子'''」と呼ばれていると述べており<ref name="heibon_1997_90">平凡社[1997: 90]</ref>、他に『紀伊名所図会』にも同様の記述が見られる<ref name="Kadokawa_1985_118"/>。これは当地に井関王子以外にも津兼王子があったとする伝承があり、この2社の異同に関する異説があったことによるものである。『紀伊続風土記』や『紀伊名所図会』は両社が同一説を採るが、2社が別々の社であったとする説もある。後者の説によれば、井関王子址の東300メートルの地が津兼王子址であり、街道筋が西よりに付け替えられたことにより、井関王子が成立したのだという<ref name="heibon_1997_90"/>。
[[明治時代|明治期]]に井関の稲荷明神社祭礼の際の御旅所とされ、村有の耕作地を社地の一部に取り込んで拡張したが、[[1909年]]（[[明治]]42年）に稲荷明神社とともに上津木八幡神社に合祀された<ref name="heibon_1997_90"/>。[[西律]]が[[1971年]]（昭和46年）に調査した際には、陶製の小さな祠がミカン畑のなかにあった<ref>西[1987: 116]</ref>が、湯浅御坊道路の工事で社地は完全に失われた<ref>長谷川[2007: 83]</ref>。
近隣の丹賀大権現に合祀されている。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町3113-1
=== 河瀬王子 === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|河瀬王子]] 井関王子から南下し、河瀬橋を渡った広川西岸にあるのが'''河瀬王子'''（ごのせおうじ）の跡地である。
「熊野道之間愚記」建仁元年（1201年）10月10日条に、井関王子についで「ツノセ王子」に参拝したとあり、『[[民経記]]』承元4年（1210年）4 月26日条には「角瀬川」と見える。しかし、この王子の呼称には異説が多く、西によれば川瀬王子（かわせおうじ、『紀伊続風土記』『紀伊名所図会』）、津の瀬王子（つのせおうじ、[[応永]]34年〈[[1427年]]〉の『熊野詣日記』）、角瀬王子（『南紀神社録』）などがあり、『和歌山県聖蹟』は「熊野道之間愚記」を根拠にツノセを本来の名としている<ref>西[1987: 117]</ref>。[[1908年]]（明治41年）に上津木八幡神社に合祀された<ref>長谷川[2007: 84]</ref>。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町河瀬143
=== 馬留王子 === 河瀬王子から南下し、鹿瀬（ししがせ）山麓にあるのが'''馬留王子'''（うまどめおうじ）の跡地である。「熊野道之間愚記」、『[[中右記]]』、さらに応永34年（1427年）の『熊野詣日記』にも記述が見えないことから、これらの参詣記の年代以降に成立したと見られる。しかし、『紀伊続風土記』は馬留の名の由来を、熊野御幸の時代に、この先の鹿瀬峠が険しいために馬で越えることが出来ず、馬を留めたことにあるとしている<ref>平凡社 [1997: 115]</ref>。[[1942年]]（[[昭和]]17年）の『[[和歌山県聖蹟]]』には、1メートル角位の小さな社<ref>長谷川[2007: 85]</ref>や数個の階段石、社殿跡と見られる玉砂利があったというが、1971年（昭和46年）に西が調査した際には、一帯はミカン畑となっており何もなかったという<ref>西[1987: 118]</ref>。[[日高郡 (和歌山県)|日高郡]][[日高町 (和歌山県)|日高町]]にある同名の[[九十九王子 (日高町)#馬留王子|馬留王子]]と区別するために、広川町の馬留王子を東ノ馬留王子、日高町の馬留王子を西ノ馬留王子と称することがある<ref>長谷川[2007: 85-87]</ref>。
* 所在地 - 和歌山県有田郡広川町399
== 周辺情報 == 馬留王子（東ノ馬留王子）から次の沓掛王子（日高町）の間にあるのが[[鹿ヶ瀬峠]]になる。紀伊路の中では珍しく石畳路が残されており、大峠と小峠の二つのピークを越えると日高町となる。以下の画像では峠を越えた日高町側も掲出する。 <gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|鹿ヶ瀬峠への道 File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|峠の頂上「法華の壇」 File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|鹿ヶ瀬峠からの道（日高町） File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|路傍の題目板碑（日高町） </gallery>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft}}
== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft}}
== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

revision.text:
This is a list of some of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子|1=Kujūku Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|1=Kujūku Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft}}
== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

== What is Kujuku Ōji? == {{Main|Kujuku Ōji}}
Kujuku Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[Kishū Domain]] during the [[Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[Meiji period]]'s shift towards [[State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Kujuku Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Kujuku Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Kujuku Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[Meiji period]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
