{{Infobox religious building|prefecture={{ill|Hirogawa|qid=Q1345650}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370043]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:52, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

revision.text:
{{Infobox religious building|prefecture={{ill|Hirogawa|qid=Q1345650}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370043]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:52, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

{{Infobox religious building|prefecture={{ill|Hirogawa|qid=Q1345650}}}}{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11370043]] Wikidata name: (none) [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:52, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} This is a list of some of the {{ill|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|fr|Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|2=ja|3=九十九王子|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|4=fr|5=Kujūkuōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|1=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=99 ōji Shrines|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninety-Nine Ōji|lt=Ninety-Nine Ōji|qq=}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=Hirokawa Town|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrine (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.

== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>

This article covers the ōji Shrines in the region of {{ill|Hirokawa Town|ja|広川町|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hirokawa Town|qq=|1=hirogawachou|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11485375}}
== What is Ninety-Nine Ōji? == {{Main|Ninety-Nine Ōji}}
Ninety-Nine Ōji Shrines (九十九王子) refers to a group of shrines along the [[Kumano Kodō|Kumano Kodo]], especially on the [[Kiiji|Kiiji and Nakahechi routes]], rapidly organized by Kumano Shugendo practitioners between the 12th and 13th centuries to guide imperial family members and nobles on their pilgrimages to Kumano. These shrines were established to pray for the protection of pilgrims.
However, after the [[:en:Jōkyū War|Jōkyū War]] in 1221, pilgrimages from Kyoto declined, leading to the deterioration of the Kiiji route. This trend continued during the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], with the Kumano pilgrimage losing its former prominence. Although there were efforts by the [[:en:Kishū Domain|Kishū Domain]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] to revive its importance, it never regained its original influence. Furthermore, the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]]'s shift towards [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]], shrine mergers, and urbanization led to the loss or obscurity of many shrine sites.
This article focuses on the Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines located in Hirogawa Town.
== Ninety-Nine Ōji in Hirogawa Town == There are three Ninety-Nine Ōji shrines in Hirogawa Town.
=== Iseki Ōji === [[File:津兼王子跡.jpeg|thumb|150x150px|Iseki (Tsugane) Ōji Site]] [[File:丹賀大権現 合祀井関王子.jpeg|thumb|Iseki Ōji enshrined at Danga Daigongen]] South of [[Kumezaki Ōji]] along the Hiro River, the remains of '''Iseki Ōji''' (井関王子) can be found near the toll gate of the [[Yuasa-Gobo Road]]. Mentioned in the "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" (part of the [[Meigetsuki]]) dated October 10, 1201, it records pilgrims resting there after praying due to the rain.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]'s "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the shrine site was said to be at the northern entrance of the village, covering 82 [[:en:Ken|Ken]] in circumference, and also referred to as '''Tsugane Ōji''' (津兼王子). While some believe Iseki and Tsugane Ōji were the same, others argue they were separate shrines. According to the latter view, Tsugane Ōji was located about 300 meters east of Iseki Ōji.
During the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], it served as an o-tabisho (temporary resting shrine) during Inari Myōjin festivals and was later merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine in 1909. The shrine site was lost during the construction of the Yuasa-Gobo Road, but Iseki Ōji is now enshrined at Danga Daigongen.
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 3113-1
=== Kawase Ōji === [[File:河瀨王子.jpg|thumb|Kawase Ōji]] South of Iseki Ōji, across the Kawase Bridge on the western bank of the Hiro River, lies the site of '''Kawase Ōji''' (河瀬王子).
The "Kumano Dō no Ma Guki" dated October 10, 1201, mentions worship at "Tsunose Ōji" after Iseki Ōji. The shrine is also referred to as "Kawase Ōji" or "Tsunose Ōji" in other historical records. In 1908, it was merged with Kamitsugi Hachiman Shrine.
* Location: Kawase 143, Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture
=== Umadome Ōji === South of Kawase Ōji, at the foot of Shishigase Mountain, lies the site of '''Umadome Ōji''' (馬留王子).
Although not mentioned in early pilgrimage records, it likely originated after these accounts. According to the "Kii Zoku Fudoki," the name "Umadome" (literally "horse stop") derives from the difficulty of crossing the steep Shishigase Pass, where travelers had to leave their horses behind. By 1942, remnants of the shrine, including small stone steps and gravel, were reported, but these had vanished by the 1970s.
To distinguish it from another Umadome Ōji in [[Hidaka Town]], this one is sometimes referred to as the "Eastern Umadome Ōji."
* Location: Hirogawa Town, Arida District, Wakayama Prefecture 399
== Surrounding Information == Between Umadome Ōji and the next [[Kutsukake Ōji]] in Hidaka Town lies the [[Shishigase Pass]], featuring rare cobblestone paths and scenic peaks.
<gallery> File:Kiiji - Kotoge 02.jpg|Path to Shishigase Pass File:Kiiji - Shikagase toge 02.jpg|Summit known as "Hokke no Dan" File:Kiiji Cobblestones 01.jpg|Path from Shishigase Pass (Hidaka Town) File:Kiiji, Itabi.jpg|Stone monument along the road (Hidaka Town) </gallery>
